Electrical engineering

 Home
OurBigBook.com Words: 19k Articles: 245
Electrical engineering designs systems that generate, transmit, measure and control electrical energy and information. An electrical circuit makes this concrete: resistors, capacitors and inductors turn electric potential differences into predictable electric currents and time-dependent responses. Signal processing then asks which information those responses preserve, suppress or reveal.
The connection is useful in both directions. A series RLC circuit selects a band of frequencies through its physical dynamics; a moving average selects frequencies by arithmetic on recorded samples. Both can be studied through a frequency response. The models differ, but the question is shared: what happens to each component of the input, and what does that do to the output we care about?

Radar

Words: 180 Articles: 3
Electrical engineering OurBigBook.com
Detection and inference about remote objects using transmitted radio waves and their returned electromagnetic radiation. A received signal depends on propagation, directional antenna gain, target scattering and receiver sensitivity.

Monostatic radar equation (PR​=PT​G2λ2σback​/[(4π)3D4])

Words: 69
Radar OurBigBook.com
For a far-field free-space link with one reciprocal antenna transmitting and receiving at range D, the outward intensity is PT​G/(4πD2). The backward scattered intensity at the receiver is this times σback​/(4πD2). Multiplying by the matched antenna effective area Gλ2/(4π) gives the displayed received power. Attenuation, misalignment and polarization mismatch require additional factors. The threshold for a root mean square voltage Vm​ across a real matched load R is Vm2​/R.

Radar cross section (σback​=4π(dσ/dΩ)back​)

Words: 86 Articles: 1
Radar OurBigBook.com
The monostatic radar cross section is 4π times the backward differential scattering cross-section. Equivalently, σback​=limr→∞​4πr2Sback​/Sinc​. It is a directional scattering measure with dimensions of area, not generally the geometric area or the total scattering cross-section. The definition may additionally specify the transmitted and received polarizations.

Electric-dipole radar cross section of a small conducting sphere (σback(e)​=4πk4a6)

Words: 42
Radar cross section OurBigBook.com
Retaining only the electric dipole induced in a small sphere gives p=4πϵ0​a3Einc​. In the backward direction its differential scattering cross-section is k4a6, so the radar cross section is 4πk4a6. This response model omits the sphere's induced magnetic dipole moment; it must be distinguished from perfect-conductor sphere dipole interference.

Analog-to-digital converter

Words: 369 Articles: 6
Electrical engineering OurBigBook.com
An analog-to-digital converter produces a discrete numerical code from an input voltage. Its specifications include input range, resolution, conversion rate, input impedance, offset, gain error and nonlinearity. A uniform b-bit converter covering voltage span Vspan​ has nominal spacing q≃Vspan​/2b. The uniform-quantization error bound applies to rounding inside the range, while clipping is a different error. Sampling and quantization are separate operations: neither sufficient sampling rate nor a large bit count alone guarantees accurate reconstruction.

Oversampling (fs​>2B)

Words: 51
Analog-to-digital converter OurBigBook.com
oversampling takes samples faster than the minimum rate required by the desired signal bandwidth. With suitable uncorrelated conversion noise, digital filtering removes noise outside that bandwidth before decimation. Independent-error averaging improves standard deviation as N−1/2; fourfold averaging ideally gains one bit of amplitude resolution. Repetition of an unchanged biased code does not produce the same benefit.

Dither

Words: 117 Articles: 1
Analog-to-digital converter OurBigBook.com
dither is an intentionally introduced fluctuation that makes a quantizer's output vary between codes, reducing signal-correlated quantization artifacts. A suitable distribution can make the averaged code carry information about a constant voltage smaller than one conversion step. The improvement requires filtering or averaging; extra noise does not improve an individual conversion or repair arbitrary calibration errors.

Sub-step estimation with uniform dither (Var(Q​)=f(1−f)Δ2/N)

Words: 64
Dither OurBigBook.com
Let a constant input lie a fraction f of the way between two consecutive quantizer levels separated by Δ. With independent uniform additive dither spanning one step and nearest-level rounding, the two output codes occur with probabilities 1−f and f. Their mean equals the input and their sample-average variance is the displayed expression. This simple model shows both the sub-step information and the remaining noise cost.

Uniform quantization error (σϵ​=Δ/12​)

Words: 94 Articles: 1
Analog-to-digital converter OurBigBook.com
rounding an unclipped voltage to equally spaced levels of separation Δ leaves error in [−Δ/2,Δ/2]. If the fractional position within a conversion interval is uniformly distributed, direct integration gives zero mean and expectation value ⟨ϵ2⟩=Δ2/12. This is a statistical model for the error, not a claim that the converter adds independent white noise for every possible input.

High-resolution quantization approximation

Words: 42
Uniform quantization error OurBigBook.com
A smooth input probability density varying slowly on the scale of one conversion interval makes the fractional uniform quantization error approximately uniform. Large overall variance is not sufficient: discrete inputs aligned with conversion levels provide a counterexample. Clipping, coarse sampling and correlations between error and signal require separate analysis.

Bit-depth requirements for waveform digitization

Words: 37
Analog-to-digital converter OurBigBook.com
A full-scale range VFS​ and allowed quantization step Δ require b≥⌈log2​(VFS​/Δ)⌉ bits. The ideal uniform-quantizer rms error is approximately Δ/12​. Bandwidth determines the sampling-rate requirement, but does not by itself determine a bit depth.

Transmission line

Words: 686 Articles: 12
Electrical engineering OurBigBook.com
A transmission line guides travelling voltage and current waves. Its distributed electrical properties determine its characteristic impedance. A mismatch at a terminal produces reflected waves; available power, delivered power and returned power are distinct quantities.

Finite impedance section of a transmission line (T=[1+(α2−1)2sin2(ωℓ/v)/(4α2)]−1)

Words: 53
Transmission line OurBigBook.com
A length ℓ with impedance ratio α between identical matched lossless lines has multiple internal reflections. Summing their amplitudes gives the displayed power transmission when the propagation speed is the same in all sections. It is unity at half-wave resonances even though either individual interface reflects. Matched remote terminations remove external echoes but not this frequency dependence.

Alternating-impedance transmission line

Words: 172 Articles: 2
Transmission line OurBigBook.com
A periodic lossless line can consist of equal-length sections with impedances Z1​,Z2​. Its semi-infinite input is a fixed point of the two-section impedance transformation. The physical solution selects a forward-energy or decaying Bloch wave. At special frequencies where the cell matrix is the identity, the fixed-point equation alone loses uniqueness; limiting absorption or a termination specifies the response.

Transmission-line stop band (∣trM/2∣>1)

Words: 61
Alternating-impedance transmission line OurBigBook.com
For a real-frequency lossless reciprocal periodic line, a cell transfer matrix has determinant one. If half its trace lies outside [−1,1], the Bloch multipliers are real reciprocal numbers rather than unit-modulus propagation factors. The physical interior field decays and carries no net power to infinity. A real reference line is then totally reflected by a semi-infinite structure; a finite structure can still tunnel.

Bloch impedance (ZB​=V/I)

Words: 55
Alternating-impedance transmission line OurBigBook.com
The voltage-to-current ratio of a selected Bloch eigenmode at a specified position within a periodic cell. It depends on the chosen cell boundary, unlike the cell's propagation eigenvalues. In a pass band a physical semi-infinite mode carries positive real power; in an ideal stop band its input impedance is reactive and the mode decays into the line.

Periodic resistive loading of a transmission line

Words: 115 Articles: 1
Transmission line OurBigBook.com
A shunt electrical resistance R inserted between the conductors of a uniform lossless transmission line of characteristic impedance Z has voltage reflection coefficient r=−Z/(2R+Z) and transmission amplitude t=1+r. Equally spaced shunts produce coherent reflected waves. The round-trip phase between neighbours is 2kL, so interference repeats in frequency with spacing vp​/(2L) for nondispersive phase speed vp​.

Single-return approximation for periodic line reflections (Rfirst​=r/[1−t2e2ikL])

Words: 67
Periodic resistive loading of a transmission line OurBigBook.com
Summing only paths that reflect at one shunt, with all previous shunts crossed once in each direction, gives a geometric series with ratio t2e2ikL. This is not the full multiple-reflection solution: it excludes paths that bounce between distinct shunts. For a semi-infinite array the exact amplitude instead obeys R=r+t2e2ikLR/(1−re2ikLR). Near coherent reflection peaks the omitted paths need not be small, even if each shunt is weak.

Standing wave ratio (SWR=(1+∣Γ∣)/(1−∣Γ∣))

Words: 56
Transmission line OurBigBook.com
On a uniform lossless transmission line, incident and reflected sinusoidal waves give voltage maxima ∣V+∣(1+∣Γ∣) and minima ∣V+∣(1−∣Γ∣). Their ratio is the voltage standing wave ratio, (1+∣Γ∣)/(1−∣Γ∣), where Γ is the voltage-wave reflection coefficient. A matched termination gives one, while perfect reflection gives an infinite ratio. These expressions assume a common real characteristic impedance and no propagation attenuation between the compared extrema.

Parallel-plate transmission line (C′=εa/d,L′=μ0​d/a)

Words: 68
Transmission line OurBigBook.com
Two perfectly conducting wide strips of width a and separation d≪a, filled with a homogeneous nonmagnetic dielectric of absolute permittivity ε, support a transverse electromagnetic mode. Ignoring edge fields, their distributed capacitance is C′=εa/d and distributed external inductance is L′=μ0​d/a. The magnetic-energy integral μ0​(I/a)2ad/2=L′I2/2 gives the latter. Their characteristic impedance is Z0​=(d/a)μ0​/ε​ and propagation speed is 1/μ0​ε​. These parameters are per unit length, distinct from a lumped capacitor and inductor.

Telegrapher's equations (Vx​=−R′I−L′It​,Ix​=−G′V−C′Vt​)

Words: 117 Articles: 1
Transmission line OurBigBook.com
A distributed transmission line with per-unit-length series resistance R′, series inductance L′, shunt conductance G′ and shunt capacitance C′ obeys the displayed coupled first-order equations by applying Kirchhoff's voltage law and Kirchhoff's current law to a short element. With R′=G′=0, both voltage and current satisfy a wave equation with speed 1/L′C′​ and characteristic impedance L′/C′​. The quantities R′,L′,G′,C′ are distributed parameters, not a single lumped resistor or capacitor.

Low-loss transmission-line attenuation (α=R′/(2Z0​)+G′Z0​/2)

Words: 59
Telegrapher's equations OurBigBook.com
For per-length line parameters R′,L′,G′,C′ and e−iωt convention, a forward factor e−Γz has Γ2=(R′−iωL′)(G′−iωC′). Expanding about the lossless limit with R′≪ωL′ and G′≪ωC′ gives Γ≃α−iωL′C′​, with Z0​=L′/C′​ and the displayed amplitude attenuation. Power decays twice as fast in the exponent. Terminal reflection is a separate power-return mechanism and need not be dissipative.

Characteristic impedance (Z0​=V+/I+)

Words: 75 Articles: 1
Transmission line OurBigBook.com
The characteristic impedance is the voltage-to-current ratio of a single forward travelling wave on a uniform transmission line. For real Z0​ and a real load resistance RL​, the voltage-wave reflection coefficient is (RL​−Z0​)/(RL​+Z0​) and the power accepted by the load is the incident power times 4RL​Z0​/(RL​+Z0​)2.

TEM travelling-wave voltage-current relation (V0​=Z0​I0​)

Words: 32
Characteristic impedance OurBigBook.com
A lossless uniform transmission line has a forward travelling-wave voltage and current related by V0​=Z0​I0​ with Z0​=L/C​. Arbitrary independent DC voltage and current fields cannot simply acquire the same forward wave factor while retaining Maxwell consistency.

Transformer (electrical engineering)

Words: 121 Articles: 1
Electrical engineering OurBigBook.com
An electrical transformer transfers energy between windings through electromagnetic induction. Its operation depends on changing magnetic flux, rather than a static magnetic field alone.

Magnetizing reactance and reflected resistance in a transformer (Rin​=(Np​/Ns​)2RL​)

Words: 104
Transformer (electrical engineering) OurBigBook.com
For an ideal electrical transformer with turns ratio n=Np​/Ns​, the secondary load RL​ appears at the primary as n2RL​, while a source resistance Rg​ appears at the secondary as Rg​/n2. A finite magnetizing inductance Lm​ contributes a parallel branch iωLm​ at the primary; its magnitude must greatly exceed the reflected load for the loaded input to be approximately resistive. The corresponding unloaded secondary self-reactance is ωLm​/n2. That reactance is distinct from the source's transformed output resistance. A specification that simultaneously calls the loaded input matched to a small resistance and calls the primary impedance very large must distinguish these two branches.

Coaxial cable

Words: 91 Articles: 2
Electrical engineering OurBigBook.com

Poynting flux into lossy coaxial conductors

Words: 30
Coaxial cable OurBigBook.com
A small longitudinal electric field drives conductor current in a lossy coaxial line. Its cross product with the azimuthal magnetic field sends energy radially into both conductors, where it becomes heat; forward power decreases with distance.

Lossless coaxial line parameters (C′=2πϵ/ln(b/a),L′=μln(b/a)/(2π))

Words: 61
Coaxial cable OurBigBook.com
For ideal coaxial conductors of radii a<b filled with a homogeneous permittivity ϵ and magnetic permeability μ, Gauss's law gives Er​=λ/(2πϵr) and hence C′=2πϵ/ln(b/a). The magnetic field Hφ​=I/(2πr) has energy per unit length L′I2/2, giving L′=μln(b/a)/(2π). These are the external-field parameters when internal magnetic penetration into the conductors is neglected. Their product is L′C′=μϵ, and the characteristic impedance is L′/C′​=μ/ϵ​ln(b/a)/(2π).

Antenna (radio)

Words: 1k Articles: 24
Electrical engineering OurBigBook.com
An antenna couples electrical circuits to propagating electromagnetic radiation for transmission or reception.

Antenna directivity (D(Ω)=4πU(Ω)/Prad​)

Words: 46
Antenna (radio) OurBigBook.com
The antenna directivity compares angular radiated power U=dPrad​/dΩ with its average over directions. Its integral is 4π. Unlike antenna gain, it uses radiated power rather than accepted input power, so it omits dissipative losses. A narrow beam can have high directivity without a larger total radiated power.

Phased array

Words: 162 Articles: 2
Antenna (radio) OurBigBook.com
A phased array combines radiation from spatially separated antennas with controlled relative phases. Changing those phases steers the direction of constructive interference without moving the elements. For an equally spaced linear array with spacing d, free-space wavenumber k and phase increment ψ, a principal beam at angle θ0​ from the array normal satisfies ψ=kdsinθ0​ when the time dependence is e−iωt and the element drives are eijψ.

Grating lobe

Words: 54
Phased array OurBigBook.com
A grating lobe is an additional principal maximum caused by spatial sampling in a phased array. A regularly spaced linear array steered towards θ0​ also has maxima wherever sinθ=sinθ0​+mλ/d lies in [−1,1]. Taking d<λ/2 excludes such maxima for all steering angles; d=λ/2 is the usual limiting choice, with an endfire degeneracy at the extreme scan directions.

Array factor

Words: 45
Phased array OurBigBook.com
The array factor describes the interference between the elements of a phased array, separately from the radiation pattern of each element. For N identical equally spaced elements,
F(θ)=∑j=0N−1​eijχ=ei(N−1)χ/2sin(χ/2)sin(Nχ/2)​,χ=ψ−kdsinθ.
(1)
At χ=2πm the limiting value has magnitude N. The total intensity is proportional to ∣F∣2 times the single-element antenna beam pattern.

Radiation resistance (Prad​=Irms2​Rrad​)

Words: 132 Articles: 1
Antenna (radio) OurBigBook.com
Radiation resistance represents emitted electromagnetic power as a real input resistance of an antenna. It does not describe conversion to heat inside the conductor. If peak current amplitude is used, Prad​=∣I0​∣2Rrad​/2. Real ohmic loss adds a separate resistance and lowers radiation efficiency. For an ideal short uniform-current element of length d, the Hertzian dipole gives Rrad​=80π2(d/λ)2 in ohms, using the usual vacuum impedance approximation 120πΩ.

Small-loop magnetic radiation resistance (Rrad​=6πc3μ0​A2ω4​)

Words: 66
Radiation resistance OurBigBook.com
A fixed electrically small loop of area A with peak sinusoidal current I0​cosωt has magnetic moment m=AI. The magnetic dipole radiation law gives mean power μ0​A2I02​ω4/(12πc3). Defining it as I02​Rrad​/2 yields Rrad​=μ0​A2ω4/(6πc3). This equivalent resistance accounts for radiation, not heating in the conductor. Rotating the loop changes its vector moment and cannot in general be modelled by the same scalar current alone.

Friis transmission equation (Pr​/Pt​=Gt​Gr​[λ/(4πd)]2)

Words: 198 Articles: 2
Antenna (radio) OurBigBook.com
The Friis transmission equation describes a far-field free-space antenna link with aligned directions, matched polarizations and negligible additional loss. It follows by multiplying the transmitter's axial energy flux Pt​Gt​/(4πd2) by the receiver's antenna effective area λ2Gr​/(4π). A receiving impedance mismatch multiplies the available received power by 1−∣ΓL​∣2. Wavelength scaling must state which gains, apertures and impedances are held fixed.

Reciprocal Hertzian-dipole echo (Pecho​/Pt​=[G2λ2/(16π2r2)]2)

Words: 65
Friis transmission equation OurBigBook.com
Two aligned lossless Hertzian dipoles in one another's broadside radiation zone have gain G=3/2 and one-way received-power fraction η=G2[λ/(4πr)]2. If the second remains conjugately matched, its matched-load scattering of a Hertzian dipole reradiates the same power as its load absorbs. Applying the reciprocal far-field link on the return gives Pecho​=Pt​η2, proportional to r−4. The statement concerns physical dipole reradiation; a pure antenna load-mismatch echo model omits that scattering and is not interchangeable with it.

Antenna load-mismatch echo (Pecho​/Pi​=∣ΓL​∣2F2)

Words: 79
Friis transmission equation OurBigBook.com
In an ideal matched-port two-port network for an antenna pair, the incident amplitude traverses the link, reflects from the receiver's load with amplitude coefficient ΓL​, then traverses the reciprocal link again. If each one-way power transfer factor is F, the returned power fraction is ∣ΓL​∣2F2. With fixed gains, F∝λ2 and this echo scales as λ4. Actual antenna structural scattering or an existing input mismatch can add a coherent return not specified by the Friis transmission equation alone.

Antenna aperture

Words: 185 Articles: 3
Antenna (radio) OurBigBook.com
An antenna aperture describes the collecting area associated with a receiving antenna. The antenna effective area need not equal its geometric projected area.

Antenna effective area (Pav​=Aeff​S)

Words: 167 Articles: 2
Antenna aperture OurBigBook.com
The antenna effective area converts incident energy flux into available received power for a specified direction and matched polarization of an electromagnetic wave. In a lossless free-space link, a transmitter of antenna gain G at range r and a receiver of effective area Aeff​ have Pr​/Pt​=GAeff​/(4πr2). Impedance or polarization mismatch reduces the delivered power.
Antenna gain-effective-area relation (Aeff​(Ω)=λ2G(Ω)/(4π))
Words: 121 Articles: 1
Antenna effective area OurBigBook.com
For a reciprocal antenna with matched polarization and load, the available antenna effective area is proportional to the directional antenna gain. For a lossless antenna, a thermal equilibrium argument fixes the constant: one polarization of Rayleigh-Jeans law radiance gives incident power (kB​T/λ2)∫Aeff​dΩdν, and matched thermal electrical noise gives kB​Tdν. Thus ∫Aeff​dΩ=λ2. Since ∫GdΩ=4π, the displayed relation follows. Reciprocal losses multiply both area and gain by the same efficiency.
Antenna voltage comparison needs an impedance convention
Words: 57
Antenna gain-effective-area relation OurBigBook.com
Antennas with effective areas Ae,1​ and Ae,2​ receiving the same polarization-matched plane wave have available powers in that ratio. If their matched-load resistances are equal, terminal voltage magnitudes have ratio Ae,1​/Ae,2​​. With unequal matched resistances the ratio becomes Ae,1​R1​/(Ae,2​R2​)​. Open-circuit voltages additionally depend on each antenna's source impedance. Geometry alone therefore fixes available-power estimates more directly than unspecified terminal voltages.

Antenna gain (G(r)=4πr2Sr​/Pin​)

Words: 75 Articles: 1
Antenna (radio) OurBigBook.com
Antenna gain compares the far-field energy flux in a specified direction with the flux that an isotropic radiator would produce using the same input power. Thus Sr​=GPin​/(4πr2). Gain includes radiation efficiency; it must be distinguished from a voltage or current amplifier gain and from directivity when losses matter.

Radiation efficiency (ηrad​=Prad​/Pin​)

Words: 29
Antenna gain OurBigBook.com
The fraction of accepted input power radiated by an antenna. With consistent feed definitions, antenna gain is radiation efficiency times antenna directivity. Ohmic losses reduce the efficiency, while feed mismatch is usually tracked separately.

Antenna temperature (TA​)

Words: 45
Antenna (radio) OurBigBook.com
The antenna temperature expresses the noise power delivered by a receiving antenna as an equivalent input noise temperature. It depends on the sky and surroundings weighted by the antenna beam pattern, as well as losses in the antenna; it need not be the physical temperature of either the antenna or a single astronomical source.

Antenna beam pattern

Antenna (radio) OurBigBook.com

Pointing tolerance of a circular receiving aperture (sinθ1/2​≃0.5145λ/D)

Words: 63
Antenna beam pattern OurBigBook.com
For a uniformly illuminated circular aperture of diameter D, normalized received power is [2J1​(x)/x]2 with x=πDsinθ/λ. The first null has sinθ=1.21967λ/D and the half-power point has sinθ≃0.5145λ/D. A pointing tolerance must name the tolerated power loss; the first-null angle is not a good low-loss tolerance. These estimates require an ideal aperture pattern and are only approximate for a dish a few wavelengths across.

Gaussian antenna beam solid angle (ΩA​≃2πα2)

Words: 48
Antenna beam pattern OurBigBook.com
For a narrow angular power pattern exp[−(u2+w2)/(2α2)] about an equatorial beam centre, the solid angle measure is locally dudw. Extending the small lobe to the plane gives its beam solid angle ΩA​≃2πα2. Both sides of the azimuthal lobe must be included. A lossless antenna then has peak antenna gain G0​≃2/α2 and peak antenna effective area A0​≃λ2/(2πα2).

Antenna (radio) OurBigBook.com

Hertzian dipole (p(t)=p(t)z)

Words: 307 Articles: 3
Dipole antenna OurBigBook.com
A Hertzian dipole is an ideal electrically short oscillating electric dipole used to model radiation from a localized current element. In vacuum its far-field electric dipole radiation has sin2θ angular power distribution and total power P=μ0​∣p¨​∣2/(6πc), evaluated at the retarded time. The electric-dipole approximation for radiation requires a source much smaller than its radiation wavelength.
Hertzian dipole fixed-current power scaling (P∝I02​ℓ2/λ2)
Words: 63
Hertzian dipole OurBigBook.com
A uniform electrically short current element of length ℓ with sinusoidal peak current I0​ has electric dipole moment amplitude p0​=I0​ℓ/ω. The mean electric dipole radiation power is ω4p02​/(12πϵ0​c3), so fixing current makes it proportional to ℓ2ω2, rather than ℓ2ω4. Current, charge excursion and dipole moment are different quantities to hold fixed when comparing antennas. The approximation requires ℓ≪λ and does not impose the nonuniform standing-current profile of a long antenna.
Oblique coupling of parallel Hertzian dipoles (PL​=P(23​sin2θ)2(4πrλ​)2)
Words: 62
Hertzian dipole OurBigBook.com
For lossless parallel Hertzian transmitting and receiving dipoles separated by distance r at angle θ to their common axis, directional gains are each G=3sin2θ/2. The emitted polarization matches the receiving axis's transverse projection. Matched-load power is therefore PL​=P[3sin2θ/2]2[λ/(4πr)]2. One angular factor describes transmission and the other reception. This assumes reciprocal ideal dipoles, conjugate matching, far-field separation and negligible dissipative loss.
Matched-load scattering of a Hertzian dipole (Psca​=Pload​)
Words: 138
Hertzian dipole OurBigBook.com
For a lossless ideal Hertzian dipole driven by an incident wave, use its induced open-circuit voltage and its feed impedance Rrad​+iX. A conjugately matched load has impedance Rrad​−iX. The same induced current therefore delivers equal power to the load and to radiation resistance: Psca​=Pload​. The scattered wave has the usual dipole angular pattern. In direction of gain G, its scattering cross-section is GAeff​, since the load receives Sinc​Aeff​.
This ideal single-mode scattering is not the same as a signal that travels through an already matched antenna port, reflects from a mismatched terminating load, and returns. A zero port reflection coefficient removes that latter echo but does not make the physical dipole invisible to the incident field. Additional structural scattering, ohmic loss or a different load changes the result.

Amplitude modulation

Words: 2k Articles: 9
Electrical engineering OurBigBook.com
Amplitude modulation encodes a message by varying the multiplying wave amplitude of a carrier wave. Conventional AM adds a positive constant before multiplication, allowing a simple envelope detector to recover the message within its limits. Multiplication translates the message's frequency spectrum into a band around the carrier, adapting a slow message to a faster channel. This is an application of the modulation property of the Fourier transform.[ref]
For an original single-message-frequency voltage model, choose
s(t)=A[1+mcos(Ωt)]cos(ωc​t),A>0,0<Ω<ωc​,m≥0.
(2)
Here t is time, A is the peak voltage amplitude of the unmodulated carrier wave, ωc​ is its angular frequency, Ω is the message angular frequency, and m is the dimensionless AM modulation index. The message shape is cos(Ωt); m measures how deeply it changes the multiplying factor. Define the signed factor q(t)=1+mcos(Ωt). The nonnegative wave envelope of the representation z(t)=Aq(t)eiωc​t is
E(t)=∣z(t)∣=A∣q(t)∣.
(3)
The instantaneous voltage s(t) crosses zero every carrier cycle, even when E(t) is large. Its value at one time, its wave envelope, and its carrier-component amplitude are three different quantities. The narrow-envelope intuition additionally needs Ω≪ωc​; the algebraic model only assumes Ω<ωc​.
The beauty is that two views reveal different parts of the same operation. In time, the message appears to ride on the oscillations. In the frequency spectrum, amplitude modulation sidebands show it as a pair of translated components. An envelope detector reads their combined shape without needing the carrier's wave phase; coherent demodulation instead uses a synchronized reference and preserves the signed factor.

Single-sideband modulation

Words: 48
Amplitude modulation OurBigBook.com
Single-sideband modulation transmits one of the two translated message bands generated by amplitude modulation. For a real signal, the transmitted negative-frequency band is the complex conjugate of the positive-frequency band. Removing the redundant band reduces the required signal bandwidth. The carrier wave may also be suppressed; its retention or removal must be specified separately.

AM modulation index (m)

Words: 170
Amplitude modulation OurBigBook.com
In the single-sinusoid AM voltage model, m is the peak fractional excursion of the signed multiplying factor from its mean value 1. At m=0 there is only the carrier wave; at m=0.5 its multiplying factor ranges from 0.5 to 1.5; at m=1 it just touches zero. For 0≤m≤1, the wave envelope extrema are
Emax​=A(1+m),Emin​=A(1−m),m=Emax​+Emin​Emax​−Emin​​.
(4)
The last equality follows by adding and subtracting the first two. An oscilloscope estimate uses local carrier peaks near the message extrema and needs enough carrier cycles to approximate those bounds. Consistent local peak-to-peak amplitude readings give the same ratio because their common factor of two cancels. Mixing a peak reading with a peak-to-peak reading does not.
For A=2V and m=0.5, the wave envelope ranges from 1 to 3V, giving (3−1)/(3+1)=0.5. These are model values. At m=1.4, the signed factor has minimum −0.4, but the nonnegative wave envelope reaches zero at its sign changes; the extrema formula would misleadingly report 1. It cannot measure the true depth of overmodulation from the folded envelope alone.

Amplitude modulation sidebands (ωc​±Ω)

Words: 459 Articles: 1
Amplitude modulation OurBigBook.com
Apply the product-to-sum formula to the voltage model:
s(t)=Acos(ωc​t)+2Am​cos((ωc​+Ω)t)+2Am​cos((ωc​−Ω)t).
(5)
The carrier wave component has peak voltage amplitude A; each AM sideband has peak voltage amplitude Am/2. These are temporal frequency spectrum components, unlike the spatial sidebands used in pattern stability. The separation Ω>0 makes the three positive angular frequencies distinct, and Ω<ωc​ keeps the lower one positive. The span between sidebands is 2Ω, or 2fm​ in hertz when fm​=Ω/(2π); this is the single-tone span, not a universal signal bandwidth for arbitrary messages.
A one-sided cosine-amplitude display assigns A to the carrier line. A two-sided complex-exponential expansion instead assigns A/2 at each of ±ωc​, and Am/4 at each of the four sideband locations. The signal is identical; confusing the conventions creates a factor-of-two error. An ideal infinite-duration sinusoid gives a spectral line. A finite recording and finite analyser resolution broaden the displayed peak.
For a voltage applied across an ideal resistor of electrical resistance R>0, a component of peak voltage B has root mean square voltage B/2​ and mean power B2/(2R) by Ohm's law. Thus
Pc​=2RA2​,P+​=P−​=8RA2m2​=4m2​Pc​,Ptot​=Pc​(1+2m2​).
(6)
The proof of additivity is to average s(t)2/R over a long time: cross-products of distinct frequencies have zero mean. Consequently the whole signal's root mean square voltage is A(1+m2/2)/2​, not simply its maximum wave envelope divided by 2​. The carrier-component A/2​ remains unchanged as m varies.
With A=2V, R=50Ω and m=0.5, the carrier supplies 40mW and each 0.5V peak sideband supplies 2.5mW, giving 45mW total. At m=1.4 each sideband is 1.4V peak and supplies 19.6mW, giving 79.2mW total. Neither case changes the carrier-component power.
The fraction of mean power in the message-bearing sidebands is m2/(2+m2). It is 1/9 at m=0.5 and 1/3 at m=1. Conventional AM spends the remaining power on a carrier that enables an inexpensive envelope detector. Increasing m beyond 1 increases this fraction in the linear model but breaks ordinary envelope recovery. Removing the carrier gives suppressed-carrier amplitude modulation and changes the receiver requirement.

Fourier filtering of overlapping amplitude-modulation sidebands

Words: 93
Amplitude modulation sidebands OurBigBook.com
The modulation property of the Fourier transform adds shifted copies of the message spectrum. If those copies overlap, their complex amplitudes add before taking a magnitude; a frequency filter then acts on this sum. For a real even triangular message spectrum proportional to (1−∣ω∣)+​ and carrier frequency 1/2<Ω<1, the translated spectra overlap over ∣ω∣<1−Ω. A filter retaining ∣ω∣<Ω therefore leaves a central plateau and sloping outer sections, rather than two disjoint triangular bands. Spectral Dirac delta lines at the cutoff need an explicitly specified filter gain: multiplying a distribution by a discontinuous mask is not defined by pointwise reasoning alone.

Overmodulation (m>1)

Words: 147
Amplitude modulation OurBigBook.com
For this single-tone AM model, overmodulation means m>1. The signed factor q(t) becomes negative whenever cos(Ωt)<−1/m. On such intervals,
Aq(t)cos(ωc​t)=A∣q(t)∣cos(ωc​t+π).
(7)
The sign reversal is a π radian shift of the carrier's wave phase. At each zero of q, the wave envelope vanishes and that phase is undefined. The waveform itself is continuous: the formula has not clipped it or created extra spectral lines.
At m=1.4=7/5, sign changes occur at message phases Ωt=arccos(−5/7) and 2π−arccos(−5/7) within each cycle. At the trough Ωt=π, the desired signed factor is −0.4, whereas its nonnegative wave envelope is 0.4A. Ideal envelope recovery followed by subtraction of A would give −0.6A there, rather than the desired message voltage −1.4A. This is loss of polarity in the detector, not loss of the message from the full modulated signal. Actual transmitter clipping is a separate signal distortion that can generate additional spectral components.

Envelope detector

Words: 280
Amplitude modulation OurBigBook.com
An envelope detector extracts the slowly varying nonnegative wave envelope of a rapid carrier wave. In a simple electrical version a diode charges a capacitor near positive carrier peaks and an attached resistor discharges it between peaks. When 0≤m<1, ideal envelope extraction gives E(t)=A[1+mcos(Ωt)]; removing the constant A leaves Amcos(Ωt). This permits recovery without a synchronized carrier reference. Carrier injection thus trades transmitted power for simplicity.[ref]
A working peak detector needs margins as well as m<1: Emin​=A(1−m) should comfortably exceed the diode's forward-voltage scale and noise, and the time constant τ=RC must suppress carrier ripple while following a falling wave envelope. The coarse scale window is
ωc​2π​≪τ≪Ω1​.
(8)
A time constant that is too short leaves carrier ripple; one that is too long makes the discharging capacitor fall more slowly than the envelope. In the ideal zero-drop, continuous-tracking approximation, following a falling E requires E/τ≥−E′. For 0<m<1,
max0<θ<π​1+mcosθmΩsinθ​=1−m2​mΩ​,τ≤mΩ1−m2​​.
(9)
Differentiating the ratio locates its maximum at cosθ=−m. This original slope check explains why operation near m=1 is demanding even before overmodulation: the upper bound tends to zero while the need to smooth carrier cycles persists. It is an approximate circuit criterion, not a guarantee in the presence of diode drops, loading or noise. At m=0 there is no varying message to track; at m=1 ideal envelope extraction remains algebraically possible, but the simple detector has no positive trough margin.
For m>1, even an ideal noiseless envelope detector returns A∣q(t)∣. Removing its mean or its original offset cannot restore the discarded sign. A more elaborate receiver can use the retained wave phase through coherent demodulation.

Coherent demodulation

Words: 171
Amplitude modulation OurBigBook.com
Coherent demodulation recovers a message by multiplying the received signal by a reference carrier wave of the same frequency and known relative wave phase, then passing the result through a low-pass filter. For the ideal AM model and reference 2cos(ωc​t+φ),
2s(t)cos(ωc​t+φ)=Aq(t)cosφ+Aq(t)cos(2ωc​t+φ).
(10)
A unity-gain ideal low-pass filter passing 0 and Ω but rejecting 2ωc​ and 2ωc​±Ω leaves Aq(t)cosφ. Such a separating cutoff exists because Ω<2ωc​−Ω. At φ=0, subtraction of A recovers Amcos(Ωt) exactly for any finite m≥0, including overmodulation, provided the transmitter and channel preserve this linear waveform. This is the signed factor, not its absolute value.
A constant phase error scales the recovered message by cosφ: a π/3 radian error halves it, and a π/2 error removes it. A known error with nonzero cosine can be compensated in gain; a frequency mismatch makes the relative wave phase drift and no longer gives constant attenuation. The lecture illustrates synchronous multiplication, filtering and phase error.[ref]

Amplitude modulation laboratory

Words: 395
Amplitude modulation OurBigBook.com
Rice University's ELEC 332: In the Lab makes the model experimentally testable. Preparation resets the spectrum analyzer and observes an unmodulated generator output on it and an oscilloscope. A Wavetek function generator supplies external modulation. The specified 10MHz carrier and 10kHz message separate three peaks. Marker readouts give frequency and level; narrowing resolution bandwidth shows how the instrument broadens a line.[ref]
Part 3 uses an SA602 analog multiplier module. The message generator also triggers the oscilloscope; multiplier output feeds both displays. A no-offset module supplies a suppressed-carrier control. Replacing it with the offset-adding module restores the carrier; varying levels tests signal distortion. Finally a radio receives the conventional AM transmission, and varying message frequency checks that the heard tone belongs to this source. These are prescribed observations, not reported measurements.[ref]
Calibration matters: verify generator voltage at the connected input, distinguish peak from peak-to-peak amplitude and root mean square, and check analyser units and loading before comparing heights with Am/2 or power with A2m2/(8R). The unmodulated carrier is a reference control. Limited resolution can merge sidebands; generator harmonics can add peaks. Rice explicitly demonstrates both limitations in Part 1.[ref]
A complementary University of Kansas procedure, A.2 - Amplitude Modulation, calibrates the added carrier and the suppressed-carrier product separately to 4V peak-to-peak before recombining them. It holds the carrier fixed, varies modulation depth, reads envelope extrema and carrier-to-sideband power differences, then connects the demodulator and adjusts its tunable low-pass filter for recovery, comparing the output with the message. These are setup targets and comparison instructions, not measured results.[ref]
The inference combines time and frequency spectrum readouts: correct sideband spacing tests frequency translation, relative heights test modulation depth, and the recovered message tests the detector. Hardware clipping, receiver filtering and noise can spoil recovery even at m<1. Conversely failure of an envelope detector at m>1 does not demonstrate failure of a synchronized multiplier receiver. The two diagrams above illustrate the stipulated linear model only.

Frequency modulation

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Electrical engineering OurBigBook.com
Frequency modulation carries a message by changing the instantaneous frequency of a carrier wave. In the ideal model the wave amplitude stays constant: information changes the rate at which the wave phase advances. Write a real electrical signal and its chosen complex representation as
s(t)=Acosϕ(t),z(t)=Aeiϕ(t),A>0.
(11)
The wave envelope in this representation has modulus ∣z(t)∣=A throughout, although s(t) continually passes through zero. A smaller instantaneous value of s(t) therefore does not mean a smaller wave amplitude. The continuously unwrapped wave phase ϕ is measured in radians; its derivative is an angular frequency, while division by 2π gives frequency in cycles per second, or hertz.
For a message m(t) expressed as an electric potential difference, an ideal voltage-controlled oscillator has sensitivity Kf​ in hertz per volt and obeys
fi​(t)=fc​+Kf​m(t),ϕ(t)=ϕ(0)+2πfc​t+2πKf​∫0t​m(τ)dτ.
(12)
The integral is essential: putting the message directly into the wave phase gives phase modulation, whose instantaneous frequency instead depends on the message's derivative. Amplitude modulation changes the multiplying wave amplitude. These are different ways to encode the same kind of message signal.
An original slow illustration uses fc​=20Hz, message frequency fm​=1Hz, frequency deviation Δf=5Hz, and FM modulation index β=5. With zero initial wave phase,
ϕ(t)=2π⋅20t+5sin(2πt),s(t)=Acos(2π⋅20t+5sin(2πt)),fi​(t)=20+5cos(2πt).
(13)
Here t is in seconds. The instantaneous frequency stays positive, between 15 and 25Hz; the wave phase always advances. The oscillations bunch up where fi​ is large and spread out where it is small, while the wave envelope remains at A.
This separation is useful in a receiver: changing a positive multiplying wave amplitude does not change the zero crossings of cosϕ, so their timing still carries the message. Noise that moves those crossings, a vanishing wave amplitude, and frequency response distortion can still damage it. The surprising beauty of FM is that a constant wave envelope can conceal a rich frequency spectrum: the components interfere to change timing instead of the envelope's height.

Instantaneous frequency (fi​(t)=ϕ′(t)/(2π))

Words: 162
Frequency modulation OurBigBook.com
For a signal with a specified differentiable, continuously unwrapped wave phase ϕ(t), its instantaneous frequency is
fi​(t)=2π1​dtdϕ​.
(14)
Unwrapping means following successive turns instead of resetting the wave phase at 2π. Differentiating a reset phase would introduce artificial jumps. An arbitrary real signal does not by itself specify a unique amplitude-phase representation; this definition refers to the phase chosen in the model.
For the single-message-frequency FM model,
ϕ(t)=2πfc​t+βsin(2πfm​t),fi​(t)=fc​+βfm​cos(2πfm​t).
(15)
The proof is the chain rule: the derivative of the sine contributes 2πfm​, which cancels the 2π in the definition. In the 20Hz example, fi​(0)=25, fi​(1/4)=20, and fi​(1/2)=15Hz. Although the frequency offset vanishes at t=1/4, the wave phase offset is then 5 radians; the wave phase offset and its rate of change need not vanish together.
Between times t1​,t2​, the accumulated number of cycles is (ϕ(t2​)−ϕ(t1​))/(2π)=∫t1​t2​​fi​(t)dt. Thus a crossing-to-crossing measurement yields an average frequency over that interval. Its reciprocal time is only an approximation to the instantaneous frequency at one point when fi​ varies slowly over a cycle.

Frequency deviation (Δf=maxt​∣fi​(t)−fc​∣)

Words: 38
Frequency modulation OurBigBook.com
The peak frequency deviation is the largest absolute value of the instantaneous frequency offset from the chosen carrier wave frequency fc​. For fi​=fc​+Kf​Mcos(2πfm​t), it is Δf=∣Kf​∣M. It is a frequency, measured in hertz, rather than a wave phase or an exact signal bandwidth.

FM modulation index (β=Δf/fm​)

Words: 74
Frequency modulation OurBigBook.com
For a message consisting of a single sinusoid with frequency fm​>0, the FM modulation index is β=Δf/fm​. It is dimensionless and equals the peak wave phase excursion in radians in the chosen sine-phase convention. Keeping Δf=5Hz while changing fm​ from 1 to 2Hz reduces β from 5 to 2.5: the same frequency deviation acts for a shorter portion of each message cycle. A general message containing many frequencies does not have a single fm​ with this meaning.

Single-tone FM sidebands (fk​=fc​+kfm​)

Words: 430
Frequency modulation OurBigBook.com
A single-tone FM signal has components displaced from the carrier wave frequency by integer multiples of the message frequency. These are temporal sidebands; the spatial sidebands used to perturb a spatial pattern are a related but different setting. To find the temporal components, apply the Jacobi-Anger expansion to the complex representation:
eiβsinθ=∑k=−∞∞​Jk​(β)eikθ,z(t)=A∑k=−∞∞​Jk​(β)e2πi(fc​+kfm​)t.
(16)
Here Jk​ is a Bessel function of the first kind. The identity follows by setting the generating variable to eiθ in its generating function.[ref]
Taking the real part gives the exact real signal expansion
s(t)=A∑k=−∞∞​Jk​(β)cos(2π(fc​+kfm​)t).
(17)
The complex representation has a Fourier coefficient AJk​(β) at fc​+kfm​; the normalized magnitude is ∣Jk​(β)∣. The identity J−k​(β)=(−1)kJk​(β) makes upper and lower complex sideband magnitudes equal, but their signs matter when reconstructing the wave phase. A negative coefficient reverses a component's wave phase by π; an amplitude display alone hides that information.
For β=5, original evaluation gives J0​(5)≈−0.17760, J1​(5)≈−0.32758, J5​(5)≈0.26114 and J6​(5)≈0.13105. Thus there are appreciable components at 14 and 26Hz, outside the 15–25Hz range of the instantaneous frequency. There is no contradiction: instantaneous frequency describes the local rate of the combined wave phase, while the frequency spectrum describes a global superposition of constant-frequency components.
For the real signal, negative frequencies must also be accounted for: a cosine at −f equals one at f. When fc​/fm​=20, the normalized positive-frequency cosine coefficient at nfm​, n>0, is exactly Jn−20​(β)+J−n−20​(β). The second term is extremely small over the plotted range, but the figure includes it. The chosen complex representation need not have a frequency spectrum supported only at positive frequencies, even when its specified instantaneous frequency is everywhere positive.
For a nonzero FM modulation index, the ideal frequency spectrum has infinitely many sidebands. Many become tiny, but drawing only visible lines does not make the exact signal bandwidth finite. A useful engineering width must state a threshold or a retained-power fraction. For the complex representation, Parseval's identity gives a simple check:
2π1​∫02π​​eiβsinθ​2dθ=∑k=−∞∞​∣Jk​(β)∣2=1.
(18)
At β=5, the sum through ∣k∣≤6 is approximately 0.99356. Retaining those complex components captures over 99% of their squared magnitudes and spans 12Hz from 14 to 26Hz. This is a stated truncation criterion, not an exact cutoff or a universal bandwidth rule. It also explains why a diminished carrier component need not imply a diminished envelope: its contribution has been redistributed among sidebands.

Narrowband frequency modulation

Words: 97
Frequency modulation OurBigBook.com
When the FM modulation index satisfies ∣β∣≪1, a Taylor expansion gives a useful first-order approximation. With ωc​=2πfc​ and ωm​=2πfm​,
As(t)​=cos(ωc​t)−βsin(ωm​t)sin(ωc​t)+O(β2)=cos(ωc​t)+2β​cos((ωc​+ωm​)t)−2β​cos((ωc​−ωm​)t)+O(β2).
(19)
The product-to-sum formula for sines exposes a carrier and one pair of sidebands, with opposite signs for this wave phase convention. Higher sidebands are neglected, not identically absent. For β=0.1, the predicted normalized first-sideband magnitude 0.05 is close to the original exact evaluation J1​(0.1)≈0.0499375. The neglected waveform term is bounded in absolute value by β2/2=0.005, using the second-derivative bound for the cosine. Small frequency deviation relative to fc​ alone does not justify this approximation: it is Δf/fm​ that must be small.

Frequency modulation laboratory

The New Jersey Institute of Technology's Lab 2: FM Modulation, Demodulation and Bessel Zeros, Part I, prepares a voltage-controlled oscillator in low-frequency mode. A frequency counter reads its output while a buffered constant electric potential difference calibrates its sensitivity. Sweeping the control voltage checks linearity; the calibrated gain is then held fixed.[ref]
An audio oscillator replaces the constant control voltage. An oscilloscope displays the signal and its FFT frequency spectrum together. Zero modulation supplies a carrier reference. Increasing message amplitude reveals sidebands, compares their heights with the carrier, and locates a carrier minimum. These readouts test the spectrum and infer frequency deviation. This is a student procedure, not a report of measured results.[ref]
A carrier minimum is a minimum of one Fourier coefficient, not disappearance of the whole signal. In the ideal model the first positive zero of J0​ is approximately β=2.4048256, while the wave envelope remains A. The lab's introductory special-cases paragraph agrees with this rounded value; step T12 mistakenly repeats the equal-sideband value for the carrier zero.[ref]
The interpretation also has practical limits. A finite recording limits frequency resolution; inadequate sampling can cause aliasing; and nonlinear VCO response can introduce extra components. Keeping the gain fixed and first checking linearity helps distinguish those effects from a change in FM modulation index. Wheatstone bridge

Words: 992 Articles: 5
Resistance bridge OurBigBook.com
The Wheatstone bridge has four resistor arms and two diagonals. Here the supply holds node A at constant electric potential difference Vs​>0 relative to node D, our electrical reference potential. The left path is A→R1​→B→R2​→D; the right path is A→R3​→C→Rx​→D. The unknown is Rx​, and R3​ is adjustable. A voltmeter or galvanometer connects B to C. We define its positive reading as VB​−VC​; exchanging its leads reverses the sign. All four electrical resistances are positive, the supply is ideal, and the calculation describes steady electric currents at fixed temperature.
Charles Wheatstone described the instrument in his 1843 Bakerian lecture while explicitly crediting Samuel Hunter Christie. The account from King's College London's collection identifies that attribution; the familiar name should not be read as an assertion that Wheatstone alone originated the bridge.[ref]
Wheatstone bridge balance (Rx​=R3​R2​/R1​)
Words: 141
Wheatstone bridge OurBigBook.com
First disconnect the detector. Each side is a voltage divider. Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's voltage law give the open-circuit intermediate electric potentials and their difference:
VB​=Vs​R1​+R2​R2​​,VC​=Vs​R3​+Rx​Rx​​,Voc​=VB​−VC​=Vs​(R1​+R2​R2​​−R3​+Rx​Rx​​).
(20)
Setting this difference to zero and cross-multiplying gives
R2​R3​=R1​Rx​,R2​R1​​=Rx​R3​​,Rx​=R3​R1​R2​​.
(21)
The balance compares ratios, not necessarily equal arm values or equal branch electric currents. At balance the detector carries no electric current, so Kirchhoff's current law again makes the electric current constant along each two-arm path.[ref]
For a worked null measurement, suppose R1​=1.000kΩ and R2​=2.000kΩ, and the detector null occurs at adjustable R3​=1.500kΩ. Then
Rx​=(1.500kΩ)1.000kΩ2.000kΩ​=3.000kΩ.
(22)
For Vs​=3.000V, both intermediate electric potentials are 2.000V. The left branch carries 1.000mA and the right branch 0.6667mA: the zero detector reading does not mean that the unknown carries no electric current. These are stipulated ideal values illustrating the calculation, not experimental observations.
Wheatstone bridge detector loading (Vd​=Voc​Rd​/(Rth​+Rd​))
Words: 288
Wheatstone bridge OurBigBook.com
A real voltmeter has finite input electrical resistance Rd​; a galvanometer also has a finite winding electrical resistance. Away from balance, its electric current changes both intermediate electric potentials. This is voltmeter loading when the detector is a voltmeter. Model the detector as a passive resistor, with no offset or injected electric current. Thévenin's theorem supplies the full response without pretending the connected bridge remains two independent voltage dividers.
With the detector removed, the equivalent source is Voc​. Replace the ideal supply by a wire to calculate the source electrical resistance seen between B,C: nodes A,D merge, making R1​,R2​ parallel and R3​,Rx​ parallel. Consequently
Rth​=R1​+R2​R1​R2​​+R3​+Rx​R3​Rx​​,Id​=Rth​+Rd​Voc​​,Vd​=Id​Rd​=Voc​Rth​+Rd​Rd​​.
(23)
Since the attenuation factor is strictly positive for Rd​>0, the null remains R2​R3​=R1​Rx​. A smaller detector electrical resistance reduces the measured electric potential difference off balance but does not shift the ideal null. Its electric current sensitivity instead depends on 1/(Rth​+Rd​); detector gain and resolution also matter in deciding how closely a null can be located.
In the plotted example, Rx​=1.100kΩ gives Voc​=−119.048mV and Rth​=1.02381kΩ. A detector with Rd​=1.000kΩ instead reads Vd​=−58.824mV. Using that loaded reading in the unloaded voltage divider formula would underestimate the deviation of Rx​ from 1kΩ. Balancing the bridge avoids this particular systematic measurement error.
The local derivative makes the sensitivity explicit. For R1​=R2​=R3​=R and Rx​=R+δR, the first-order Taylor expansion is
Vd​=−4RVs​​R+Rd​Rd​​δR+O((δR)2).
(24)
At the plotted null, the open-circuit slope is −1.25mV/Ω, compared with −0.625mV/Ω for Rd​=1kΩ. Increasing the supply improves this ideal sensitivity but also increases Joule heating. A finite source electrical resistance requires recomputing Rth​; the displayed parallel-pair expression assumes an ideal supply.
Slide-wire resistance bridge experiment
Words: 335
Wheatstone bridge OurBigBook.com
PHYWE's documented experiment uses a one-metre slide wire, a connection box, an unknown resistor, a known comparison resistor, a supply, and a digital multimeter in steady-current mA mode as the null detector. Its two yellow detector leads join the fixed-resistor junction and the slider. Move the slider until the indicated electric current vanishes; read the two wire lengths on the ruler and infer the unknown electrical resistance from their ratio. The guide advises changing the comparison resistor if no null is reachable or the slider lies near an end.[ref]
The inference requires uniform electrical resistivity and wire cross-sectional area, so the two wire electrical resistances have the ratio of their lengths, by R=ρel​L/A. Retaining PHYWE's labeling, its equation (6) is Rx​=RC​ℓ1​/ℓ2​, where RC​ is the comparison electrical resistance. This is a different arm placement from our schematic. The guide's example table reports larger discrepancies near wire ends.[ref]
Useful additional controls distinguish a true null measurement from an insensitive or disconnected detector. Check the detector zero with the supply off, then move the adjustable arm slightly to either side of the candidate balance and verify opposite detector signs. Reconnect the unknown with short, secure leads and repeat the balance. Any lead or contact electrical resistance included in that arm contributes to the inferred value, even though a detector lead carries no electric current at exact balance. For very small unknown electrical resistances, four-terminal sensing addresses this separate connection problem; a detector null alone does not remove it.
Check for Joule heating by repeating at lower supply electric potential difference and with shorter powered intervals, holding ambient temperature fixed. At balance the unknown still dissipates power
Px​=(R3​+Rx​Vs​​)2Rx​.
(25)
Halving Vs​ quarters this power while halving ideal detector sensitivity. A balance that moves with excitation or elapsed time suggests changing electrical resistance, including self-heating; it is not explained by passive detector loading alone. These are proposed controls, not claimed outcomes of PHYWE's experiment. Standard-resistor accuracy, wire uniformity, contact reproducibility and finite detector resolution still limit the electrical measurement. Large electrical resistances also make unwanted leakage paths consequential.

Voltage divider (Vout​=Vs​Rb​/(Ra​+Rb​))

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Electrical engineering OurBigBook.com
A voltage divider uses two resistors connected in series to obtain a fraction of an applied electric potential difference. Let the upper electrical resistance be R1​>0, the lower one R2​>0, and the input be Vin​=Vs​ relative to a common electrical reference potential. The output is the junction's electric potential difference relative to that same reference, across R2​. The familiar ratio assumes zero output electric current: no external electrical load draws from the junction. In a steady direct current model with fixed resistors obeying Ohm's law and an ideal voltage source,
I=R1​+R2​Vin​​,V0​=IR2​=Vin​R1​+R2​R2​​.
(26)
Here V0​ is the open-circuit voltage; R1​,R2​ correspond to Ra​,Rb​ in the header formula. With no junction branch, Kirchhoff's current law makes the same electric current pass through both resistors, and Ohm's law gives the two voltage drops. For Vs​=0, division gives V0​/Vs​=R2​/(R1​+R2​); if Vs​=0, the predicted output is zero but this ratio is undefined.
An original stipulated example has R1​=R2​=10kΩ and Vin​=10V. With zero output electric current, I=0.5mA and V0​=5V. An attached 10kΩ electrical load instead gives Vout​=10/3V; a 1MΩ load gives Vout​=1000/201V=4.975124378…V. These are exact model predictions, not measured readings or specifications of a particular multimeter or oscilloscope.
The divider is useful for scaling a voltage or converting a change in a sensor's electrical resistance into an electric potential difference. Its beauty is also its trap: multiplying both electrical resistances by the same positive factor preserves the unloaded ratio, but changes the effect of any fixed electrical load. A divider therefore supplies a predictable ratio under specified loading conditions; it is not a source that maintains that voltage for arbitrary output electric currents. A Wheatstone bridge compares two divider junctions, while Thévenin's theorem describes the divider's response to many different loads.

Voltage divider OurBigBook.com
Connect a passive electrical load of electrical resistance RL​>0 from the junction to the reference. In the steady direct current model, RL​ and R2​ share the same electric potential difference and are connected in parallel. Their equivalent electrical resistance is
Rp​=R2​∥RL​=R2​+RL​R2​RL​​,Vout​=Vin​R1​+Rp​Rp​​=R1​R2​+(R1​+R2​)RL​Vin​R2​RL​​.
(27)
This is the replacement required when a voltmeter is connected across R2​. The inspected teaching guide explicitly models the meter this way.[ref]
The Kirchhoff's current law proof makes the changed assumption visible:
R1​Vin​−Vout​​=R2​Vout​​+RL​Vout​​.
(28)
The upper resistor carries the sum of the lower and load electric currents, so the two original resistors no longer have equal electric currents. In the stipulated RL​=10kΩ example, Rp​=5kΩ, the upper current is 2/3mA, and each lower branch carries 1/3mA.
For a digital multimeter used as a voltmeter, let its input electrical resistance on the selected voltage range be Rm​. With no other load, set RL​=Rm​; if an intended load is also present, use RL​∥Rm​ in place of RL​. Two instruments connected simultaneously add two branches. Their ideal indicated value equals the voltage of this altered circuit; voltmeter loading can exist even with perfect measurement calibration. Real readout additionally has measurement uncertainty, offsets, and finite resolution. Consult the actual range and input specifications rather than assigning every digital multimeter the same Rm​.
For an oscilloscope, the resistance-only model applies to settled direct current with a compatible input coupling setting. The oscilloscope input and cable also have capacitance; changing signals can therefore have loading that depends on frequency. A probe changes the impedance seen at its tip and the relation between tip voltage and displayed voltage; use the probe-and-input combination's specification and attenuation setting. NJIT's guide models the parallel electrical resistance and capacitance and adjusts probe compensation with a square-wave readout.[ref]

The Thévenin resistance Rth​=R1​∥R2​ summarizes the divider's susceptibility: the relevant comparison is RL​/Rth​, not merely a large absolute RL​.

Voltage divider teaching experiment

Words: 435
Voltage divider OurBigBook.com
Southern Illinois University's ET 304A guide, Lab 4: Voltage Measurements and Meter Loading Effects, documents an instructive test: build equal-arm voltage dividers on a 20V supply, then measure across the lower arm with a digital multimeter, analog multimeter, and oscilloscope. Starting with two 10kΩ resistors, repeat with equal pairs from 220kΩ to 4.7MΩ. It requires separate recorded readings, unloaded predictions, and predictions including each instrument's input electrical resistance. The guide obtains meter resistances from specification sheets and scope resistance from the input-panel marking. Equal ratios control the unloaded target while changing susceptibility to voltmeter loading. The provided tables are blank: the guide specifies a procedure, not measured outcomes.[ref]
Preparation and accuracy checks are made concrete by Berkeley's Lab 1: Introductory Experiments and Linear Circuits I. Its different divider uses nominal 470kΩ and 10kΩ resistors and a 24V supply on a breadboard. Measure isolated resistors first, record actual supply voltage, recalculate with these measured values, then record the junction voltage with the digital multimeter. It explicitly compares actual values with resistor tolerance and the final voltage with a range-dependent accuracy bound from the instrument manual. This is an uncertainty check, not an independent measurement calibration.[ref]
For a controlled comparison, additionally record the selected instrument range, probe factor, and input coupling; connect each instrument separately to the same electrical reference potential, and monitor the input rather than treating the supply label as an exact voltage. These are proposed controls for interpreting the documented procedures. A voltage indication and a resistance indication from the same digital multimeter do not independently validate its measurement calibration; a traceable reference comparison would be needed for that. Resistor tolerance describes component variation, while measurement uncertainty describes what is known about measured values. Using nominal arms alone can confuse mismatch with loading: equal nominal arms each within one-percent tolerance can give unloaded ratios from 0.495 to 0.505.
The inference to test is specific: once actual arm values, input voltage, and meter input electrical resistance are accounted for, the readout should approach the loaded voltage divider prediction within the remaining measurement uncertainty. A discrepancy can instead reflect contacts, changing temperature, source droop, or an input that is not a fixed passive resistor. A source with positive series electrical resistance Rs​ can be modeled by replacing R1​ with R1​+Rs​ only when Vs​ denotes its ideal internal voltage; when the actual voltage across the divider is measured, that terminal value is already Vin​. During settling, or with appreciable input capacitance and changing signals, the steady direct current calculation is insufficient. Neither institutional procedure supplies measured values for the original 10V example above.

Thévenin's theorem (V=Voc​−IRth​)

Words: 2k Articles: 7
Electrical engineering OurBigBook.com
Thévenin's theorem replaces the terminal behavior of a linear resistive circuit by an ideal voltage source in series with a Thévenin resistance, whenever its terminal electric potential difference is a well-defined affine function of the delivered electric current. Fix terminals a,b, write V=ϕ(a)−ϕ(b), and take I positive out of the network at a into the electrical load, returning through b. Then
V=Voc​−IRth​.
(32)
The open-circuit voltage Voc​ is the intercept at I=0; −Rth​ is the slope. Thus two parameters predict what happens when many different electrical loads are connected. The Wheatstone bridge detector loading calculation uses precisely this replacement to find the detector reading even when the bridge's two voltage dividers interact through its detector.
For example, a 12V ideal voltage source with 2kΩ above and 4kΩ below a voltage divider junction supplies Voc​=8V and Rth​=34​kΩ at that junction relative to the lower terminal. Attaching a 4kΩ electrical load reduces its voltage to 6V and draws 1.5mA. The equivalent explains why an unloaded divider ratio alone cannot predict a loaded output.
The equivalence concerns the chosen terminals, including the power VI delivered there. It does not identify internal branch electric currents or internal Joule heating. At open circuit the original divider still draws 2mA from its 12V supply, while the equivalent's series branch carries no electric current. [ref]

Thévenin terminal response (V=Voc​−IRth​)

Words: 202
Thévenin's theorem OurBigBook.com
With the passive sign convention applied to the network, its entering electric current is J=−I, and the same relation becomes V=Voc​+JRth​. The electrical load uses the passive sign convention with entering electric current I, so it absorbs power VI. A positive delivered electric current therefore produces a voltage drop for positive Rth​; changing the reference direction without changing the equation would give the wrong sign.
The reason is linearity of Ohm's law, Kirchhoff's current law, Kirchhoff's voltage law, and the constitutive relations of any linear dependent electrical sources. Solve once at I=0 with the independent electrical sources present. Subtract this solution from a solution with prescribed delivered electric current I: the fixed independent electrical sources cancel, leaving a homogeneous linear network whose terminal voltage change is proportional to I. This is a short superposition principle argument for an affine function; the fixed offset need not vanish.
The qualification about a well-defined response matters. An ideal voltage source alone has Rth​=0. An ideal nonzero current source alone constrains I and does not have a finite open-circuit voltage or a representation V=Voc​−IRth​ with finite coefficients. Linear dependent electrical sources can give negative resistance, and singular ideal networks may fail to have a unique finite response. Neither a finite nor a strictly positive passive Rth​ follows merely from calling an electrical circuit linear. [ref]

Thévenin divider example

Words: 139

In the pictured original linear resistive circuit, the ideal voltage source keeps its upper node at 12V relative to b. Let R1​=2kΩ connect that node to a, and R2​=4kΩ connect a to b. With the external electrical load removed, the voltage divider gives
Voc​=12V2kΩ+4kΩ4kΩ​=8V.
(33)
To find the Thévenin resistance, Thévenin source suppression replaces the ideal 12V voltage source by a wire. Both resistors now join a to b in parallel, giving
Rth​=R1​+R2​R1​R2​​=34​kΩ.
(34)
This is the electrical resistance looking into the original network with its independent electrical source suppressed; the external electrical load is excluded.
An independent check uses Kirchhoff's current law at a, without suppressing anything:
2kΩ12V−V​=4kΩV​+I,V=8V−(34​kΩ)I.
(35)
The Thévenin terminal response thus follows directly from the original topology. Shorting a to b in this ideal calculation gives Isc​=6mA: the lower resistor has zero voltage and the upper resistor limits the electric current. All numerical values here and in the figures are stipulated model values, not laboratory data.

Thévenin source suppression

Words: 288
Thévenin's theorem OurBigBook.com
To determine the Thévenin resistance, remove the external electrical load and set each independent electrical source to zero in the circuit model. A zero ideal voltage source enforces zero electric potential difference, so replace it by a short connection. A zero ideal current source enforces zero electric current, so replace it by an open connection. Retain every resistor, including any explicitly modeled supply electrical resistance. Turning an actual power supply's front-panel control to zero is not evidence that it physically becomes an ideal wire.
Retain every dependent electrical source and its controlling variable: its response to an electrical test source is part of the network's electrical resistance. Impose terminal voltage vt​ with an electrical test source and calculate jt​ entering the suppressed network at a. For a nonzero test yielding a finite ratio,
Rth​=jt​vt​​.
(36)
Alternatively inject a known entering electric current and solve for vt​. The test electric current is opposite to the delivered-current convention of the original Thévenin terminal response. [ref]
For an original illustration, put a positive resistor R across a,b and a dependent electrical source in parallel that injects electric current gvt​ from b toward a, where g has units of electrical conductance. Its control is the same terminal voltage vt​. Kirchhoff's current law gives
jt​=Rvt​​−gvt​,Rth​=R−1−g1​.
(37)
With R=1kΩ and g=0.5mS, a 1V test draws 0.5mA, giving Rth​=2kΩ. Removing the dependent electrical source would falsely give 1kΩ. With g=2mS, the model instead has Rth​=−1kΩ; with g=1mS it draws zero test electric current for any imposed voltage and has no finite ratio. An active physical realization requires a supply and has a limited operating range.
For a finite nonzero Rth​ and a well-defined short-circuit response, Isc​=Voc​/Rth​. Thus Rth​=Voc​/Isc​ is usable when Isc​=0. A source-free positive resistor has both Voc​=0 and Isc​=0, so this quotient cannot reveal its electrical resistance; an electrical test source can.

Thévenin load response (VL​=Voc​RL​/(Rth​+RL​))

Words: 169
Thévenin's theorem OurBigBook.com
A positive resistive electrical load obeys Ohm's law, VL​=IRL​. Its resistive load line intersects the Thévenin terminal response at
I=Rth​+RL​Voc​​,VL​=Rth​+RL​Voc​RL​​,
(38)
provided Rth​+RL​=0. For the Thévenin divider example, RL​=1kΩ gives I=24/7mA and VL​=24/7V; RL​=4kΩ gives I=1.5mA and VL​=6V. At RL​=Rth​=34​kΩ, the voltage is 4V, half the open-circuit voltage.
For this positive Rth​, increasing RL​ reduces the drawn electric current and raises VL​ toward Voc​. This explains voltmeter loading: a voltmeter itself is an electrical load. The equivalence also applies to a nonlinear electrical load through intersection with its terminal relation, but an arbitrary load need not give a unique operating point. If negative Rth​ cancels positive RL​, the displayed formula is singular; a real active circuit's limits and dynamics must then be considered.

Thévenin measurement experiment

Thévenin's theorem OurBigBook.com
An authored teaching experiment uses an adjustable steady-voltage supply, a digital multimeter, fixed resistors, and a 10kΩ potentiometer or resistance decade box. Its original circuit uses a 10V supply and 3.3, 6.8, and 4.7kΩ resistors; the student compares 8.2 and 2.2kΩ electrical loads. The readout is load voltage, recorded against prediction and deviation. The student then removes the electrical load to measure the open-circuit voltage, disconnects the supply and substitutes a wire to measure the Thévenin resistance with the multimeter's resistance mode, and restores the supply for an independent method: adjust the variable electrical load until the voltmeter reads half the unloaded voltage. Finally the student builds the equivalent and repeats both load measurements. Its tables are blank recording forms, not reported observations. [ref]
The half-voltage inference assumes negligible voltmeter loading and positive Rth​. A finite voltmeter input electrical resistance Rm​ actually gives an apparent unloaded reading
Vm​=Voc​Rth​+Rm​Rm​​.
(39)
When the same voltmeter remains connected across a variable electrical load RL​, the network sees Rp​=RL​Rm​/(RL​+Rm​). Setting its reading to Vm​/2, rather than to the true Voc​/2, gives
RL​=Rth​+Rm​Rth​Rm​​.
(40)
Thus the uncorrected half-reading method underestimates positive Rth​. In the original 12V example, a stipulated Rm​=10kΩ gives Vm​=120/17V≈7.059V and half-reading load RL​=20/17kΩ≈1.176kΩ, instead of 34​kΩ. These are model predictions for a deliberately loading meter, not the specification or observed readout of the source experiment's instrument.
Finite readings can also estimate the terminal line without a physical short. For two distinct load settings with corrected delivered electric currents I1​,I2​ and terminal voltages V1​,V2​,
Rth​=I2​−I1​V1​−V2​​,Voc​=V1​+I1​Rth​.
(41)
If the voltmeter remains across each electrical load, the delivered electric current is Ik​=Vk​(1/RL,k​+1/Rm​), including the meter branch. Omitting it biases the inferred slope.
Useful additional controls are to measure each resistor separately before assembly, verify terminal polarity, repeat an earlier load setting to detect supply drift, and compare a third setting with the inferred Thévenin terminal response. These are proposed controls, not reported outcomes of the source experiment. Closely spaced electric currents make the slope estimate sensitive to voltage resolution and measurement error; widely separated settings may trigger source current limiting or Joule heating that changes electrical resistance. Lead and contact electrical resistance, meter input uncertainty and rounding limit the inference. An ohmmeter injects its own test electric current; its reading on a powered network is not the suppressed-network ratio. Measurements with independent sources physically removed do not characterize an active dependent electrical source whose control or supply has also been disconnected.

Signal processing transforms or analyzes signals to extract information, change a representation, or improve a measurement. Examples include smoothing a sensor record, selecting a band of frequencies, and decomposing a recording through Fourier analysis. A signal is a mathematical representation of a physical record; deciding which variation is meaningful and which is noise is part of the problem.
A linear filter offers a simple entry point. Its output is assembled from weighted copies of its input. A moving average can reduce rapid variation, but it also changes timing and can erase useful detail. The worked example below makes that tradeoff explicit rather than treating a smoother plot as automatic improvement.
Two complementary views make the subject appealing. An impulse response describes the effect of a localized input; a frequency response describes the effect of a sustained oscillation. For a linear time-invariant system, both describe the same operation, connected by convolution and Fourier analysis. [ref].

Improve a circuit's signal-to-noise ratio by reducing unwanted coupling and physical noise sources while retaining the signal bandwidth. Important methods include lowering appropriate resistances or temperature to reduce thermal electrical noise, controlling leakage and bias currents relevant to shot noise, minimizing pickup with shielding and small loop area, and selecting an operational amplifier for the source electrical impedance. Filtering limits integrated noise only if it preserves the information-bearing spectrum; a lock-in amplifier can move detection above a flicker noise region and select a narrow band. Uncorrelated noise variances add, whereas coherent pickup requires its phases and correlations to be considered. Repeated averaging reduces independent random error, but does not remove an arbitrary systematic error or slow drift.

Shot noise (SI(1)​=2qI)
Words: 2k Articles: 8
Noise (signal processing) OurBigBook.com
Shot noise is fluctuation associated with discrete transfer events. For an electric current, individual charge carriers contribute finite amounts of electric charge, even when a meter displays a smooth mean. The simplest model is a stream of equal, independently arriving charges with constant rate: its Poisson process predicts both the mean electric current and the variance around it. Discreteness alone does not imply a Poisson distribution; the timing and correlations matter.
The useful surprise is that noise can reveal something a mean hides. Two devices can carry the same mean electric current yet have different fluctuations because one transfers charges independently and the other groups or regulates them. A calibrated shot noise photocurrent measurement can connect a macroscopic voltage variance to the elementary charge. Thermal electrical noise instead exists in an unbiased resistor at thermal equilibrium; a measured background can contain both mechanisms.
Walter Schottky's 1918 paper Über spontane Stromschwankungen in verschiedenen Elektrizitätsleitern treated amplifier sensitivity limits. Part II considered independent discrete transfers, including thermionic emission through a vacuum. On p. 563 he proposed amplifying fluctuations from a separate discharge tube to determine the elementary charge; those experiments were prospective, not reported results.[ref]

Background, detector noise, variable illumination and photon correlations can invalidate that source-only formula.

For an original count example with λT=4, the mean count and its variance are both 4, the standard deviation is 2, and the relative standard deviation is 1/2. These are fluctuations of a time average, not the variance of an ideal instantaneous electric current. A model of point transfers has arbitrarily sharp impulses; it acquires a finite measured variance only after specifying a gate or linear filter. Actual collection pulses have finite duration and electrical circuits have finite response times.
