MIT's guide uses an illuminated vacuum photodiode, with collecting anode positive relative to the emitting cathode. A transimpedance amplifier gives V1​=RF​I; a multimeter reads its mean. The fluctuation path rejects below 100Hz, adds roughly tenfold voltage gain, then nominal hundredfold preamplification and a 1–50kHz band-pass filter; the readout measures root mean square voltage. With diode bias off, a sinusoid at the test port calibrates g(f). Restore bias, retain gain settings, vary lamp brightness, and repeat both readings. The guide warns about overload; it supplies a procedure, not measured results.[ref]
The inference can be expressed without relying on nominal passband edges. Let g(f) denote the calibrated voltage transfer after the RF​ conversion, so K(f)=RF​g(f) and define K=∫0∞​∣K(f)∣2df. Under independent arrivals and an unchanged additive background,
σv,measured2​(I)=2qKI+σv,background2​,q=2K1​dIdσv,measured2​​.
(55)
The slope of voltage variance against mean electric current can therefore estimate q. A free intercept accounts for a constant background; forcing the line through zero generally biases the slope. The root mean square readings must have their mean removed and then be squared. Subtracting two root mean square amplitudes does not subtract independent variances. Estimate the variance from successive records; averaging the waveforms first would suppress the fluctuation being measured.
Additional controls sharpen this interpretation. Block the light with detector bias, temperature, and gain unchanged; this preserves dark current and electronics while removing photocurrent. Repeat this dark comparison between illumination settings to check drift. If independent dark arrivals have mean magnitude Id​ and illuminated arrivals add Iph​, their spectra add: 2q(Id​+Iph​). Subtracting the unchanged dark variance isolates 2qIph​K. This subtraction model assumes unchanged transfers and independence; switching off bias for gain calibration is a different control and need not preserve the dark background.
Vary measured Iph​ rather than assuming lamp knob position is proportional to photocurrent. Check collection versus bias to identify a range where incomplete collection is negligible; a space charge limited tube can correlate transfers. Verify that the transimpedance amplifier remains linear and that its frequency response is unchanged over the illumination range. Changing signal bandwidth should change the excess variance through K; compare inferred input spectra in several bands. Correlated fluctuations of the light source can add a contribution scaling approximately as Iph2​, while an electronics floor can hide the linear term at small electric currents. A fitted line over a short range alone does not establish independent transfers.
The gain calibration must include the same detector-to-readout path used for noise, or explicitly supply any omitted transfer. Detector capacitance, finite collection time, amplifier voltage and current noise, thermal electrical noise, pickup, clipping, and finite recording precision limit the inference. Current-dependent electrical impedance or heating can make a background current-dependent too. Since K contains squared gain, a small fractional error in gain produces approximately twice that fractional error in the predicted variance scale. Knowing a nominal gain and two cutoff settings is insufficient.
Shot noise departures from Poisson statistics (FT​=Var(NT​)/E[NT​])
Words: 276
Shot noise OurBigBook.com
The Fano factor FT​ compares count variance with its mean over a specified gate. For a stationary unidirectional stream with fixed charge q, finite count second moments, and a generalized autocovariance with finite integral so that the long-gate limit exists,
F∞​=limT→∞​E[NT​]Var(NT​)​,SI(1)​(0+)=2qIF∞​.
(56)
The zero-frequency relation concerns the continuous fluctuation spectrum, excluding the mean spectral line. It follows by writing Var(QT​) as the double integral of the current autocovariance; for long T, its leading term is TSI(2)​(0). A finite-gate FT​, a frequency-dependent ratio SI(1)​(f)/(2qI), and a factor inferred from one filtered variance are not interchangeable. The last is weighted by the instrument's ∣K(f)∣2.
Two original counting counterexamples show why electric charge discreteness is insufficient. In n independent time slots, transfer one charge with probability p in each slot: the binomial distribution gives mean np, variance np(1−p) and Fano factor 1−p. A random common origin for the slots removes a preferred time origin; the long-gate factor remains 1−p. Alternatively, if independent Poisson process bursts each transfer exactly two charges, then NT​=2MT​ gives Var(NT​)=2E[NT​] and factor 2. Both count individual charges; only the first model allows at most one per slot, and the second groups them in pairs.
Consequently 2qI is a reference for independent unidirectional arrivals, not a universal noise law for all electrical conductors. Correlations, charge multiplication, and bidirectional transfer require a more specific model. For example, independent opposite streams with positive current magnitudes I+​ and I−​ have net mean I=I+​−I−​ but one-sided fluctuation spectrum 2q(I+​+I−​). Using 2q∣I∣ would miss their fluctuations when the net current is small. At thermal equilibrium, the full transport model must also respect thermal electrical noise; adding unrelated phenomenological formulas can double count the same underlying transfers.
Thermal electrical noise (vn,rms​=4kB​TRB​)
Words: 1k Articles: 6
Noise (signal processing) OurBigBook.com
Thermal electrical noise is the fluctuating electric potential difference or electric current produced by thermal fluctuations in a dissipative electrical circuit, even without an applied voltage. A resistor at thermal equilibrium is both a source of noise and a sink for electrical energy. Its electrical resistance describes the dissipation, and its absolute temperature sets the scale of the fluctuations. This connects a practical limit on signal-to-noise ratio to statistical mechanics: a warm, unbiased resistor is not electrically silent.
John Bertrand Johnson measured the effect using a vacuum-tube amplifier and thermocouple; his 1928 paper reported agreement with the Boltzmann constant. Harry Nyquist's companion paper calculated the effect from thermodynamics and statistical mechanics.[ref][ref]
Thermal noise spectral convention (Sv(1)​(f)=4kB​TR)
Words: 182
Thermal electrical noise OurBigBook.com
Model an ideal resistor of constant electrical resistance R>0 at uniform absolute temperature T by its Thévenin equivalent: a zero-mean random voltage source in series with a noiseless R. In the classical range its one-sided, open-circuit voltage power spectral density, per hertz, is
Sv(1)​(f)=4kB​TR(f≥0),[Sv(1)​]=V2/Hz,
(57)
where kB​ is the Boltzmann constant. Thus a positive-frequency interval of width df contributes 4kB​TRdf to the mean square voltage. This is approximately white noise only where the electrical resistance is effectively constant and hf≪kB​T, with h the Planck constant. The ideal constant spectrum cannot describe arbitrarily high frequencies.[ref]
For a real voltage, an equivalent two-sided power spectral density is Sv(2)​(f)=2kB​TR over signed frequencies. With a real linear time-invariant system of frequency response H(f), the same output mean square is
⟨vo2​⟩=∫0∞​Sv(1)​(f)∣H(f)∣2df=∫−∞∞​Sv(2)​(f)∣H(f)∣2df.
(58)
Angle brackets denote an expected value; for this zero-mean noise the mean square is its variance. Do not integrate 4kB​TR over both signs of frequency: that counts the same fluctuations twice. All integrals here use frequency f in hertz, not angular frequency ω=2πf. The amplitude spectral density is 4kB​TR​ in V/Hz​, whereas the root mean square voltage requires a specified measurement signal bandwidth.
Effective noise bandwidth (Bn​=∫0∞​∣H(f)∣2df/∣H0​∣2)

For a linear filter with chosen nonzero reference voltage gain H0​, define its effective noise bandwidth by
Bn​=∣H0​∣21​∫0∞​∣H(f)∣2df.
(59)
This is the width of an ideal rectangular linear filter with gain magnitude ∣H0​∣ passing the same mean square of input white noise. Consequently
vo,rms​=∣H0​∣4kB​TRBn​​.
(60)
Use the full voltage transfer from the open-circuit voltage source to the readout, including any electrical load, when applying this formula. A nominal signal bandwidth stated between two cutoff frequencies does not specify the integral: gradual tails and a nonuniform passband matter. For an ideal rectangular unit-gain passband [f1​,f2​], Bn​=f2​−f1​. For an unloaded RC low-pass filter with H0​=1 and cutoff frequency fc​=1/(2πRC),
Bn​=∫0∞​1+(f/fc​)2df​=2π​fc​=4RC1​.
(61)
The last equality follows by substituting x=f/fc​ and integrating 1/(1+x2) as arctanx. Using the nominal fc​ as the noise bandwidth underestimates the variance by a factor π/2, or the root mean square voltage by π/2​.
Thermal noise loading
Words: 170
Thermal electrical noise OurBigBook.com
An external electrical load changes the terminal noise. Connecting a purely resistive load RL​>0 to the noisy resistor gives the voltage divider ratio RL​/(R+RL​). The source resistor's contribution at the load is
SvL​(1)​(f)=4kB​TR(R+RL​RL​​)2.
(62)
In a rectangular signal bandwidth B, the power delivered by that source contribution to the load is
PR→L​=4kB​TB(R+RL​)2RRL​​≤kB​TB,
(63)
because (R−RL​)2≥0. Equality occurs at RL​=R: this is matched available noise power. Matching halves the voltage, quarters its power spectral density, and gives Pav​=kB​TB. Dividing the squared open-circuit voltage by R would instead give four times this available power.
These expressions isolate the source resistor's contribution. A real load resistor also generates thermal electrical noise. At the same temperature its independent contribution produces the equal reverse power flow, so the net thermal power transfer is zero at thermal equilibrium. For example, two equal resistors at the same temperature have total terminal power spectral density 2kB​TR, equivalent to 4kB​T(R/2). One contribution alone is kB​TR. The fictitious noiseless series R in the Thévenin equivalent is not an additional physical source: adding its noise again would double count the original resistor.

Sv(1)​=1.6567788×10−16V2/Hz,Sv(1)​​≈12.872nV/Hz​,

Represent the resistor by its noisy Thévenin equivalent. The resulting RC low-pass frequency response gives the stationary capacitor voltage power spectral density
SC(1)​(f)=1+(2πfRC)24kB​TR​.
(66)
Its mean square follows by the effective noise bandwidth calculation:
⟨vC2​⟩=4kB​TR∫0∞​1+(2πfRC)2df​=4kB​TR4RC1​=CkB​T​.

This is also the equipartition theorem: the mean capacitor energy is 21​C⟨vC2​⟩=21​kB​T. Raising R makes the low-frequency spectrum taller and its width narrower in exactly compensating proportions. It changes the equilibration time RC, not the final variance.
The integral to infinity belongs to the ideal classical model. For a physical electrical circuit, assume thermal equilibrium, linear components with negligible extra dissipation, and a corner far below the frequencies where parasitic effects, frequency-dependent electrical resistance, or hf∼kB​T invalidate the model; the omitted high-frequency tail must be negligible. A finite-bandwidth instrument measures only part of this variance. Its input capacitance contributes to the total C, and its finite input electrical resistance introduces both loading and its own thermal electrical noise.
For T=300K and C=1nF, the predicted equilibrium variance is 4.141947×10−12V2 and the root mean square voltage is 2.0352μV. At R=10kΩ, RC=10μs and Bn​=25kHz. At R=100kΩ, RC=100μs and Bn​=2.5kHz; the equilibrium root mean square voltage is identical.

⟨vC​(t)2⟩=2kB​TR∫0t​h(u)2du=CkB​T​(1−e−2t/(RC)).

The factor 2kB​TR here is the two-sided time-domain noise intensity; the equilibrium spectral integral above used the one-sided 4kB​TR. They give the same long-time limit. The variance approaches equilibrium with time constant RC/2, although a deterministic initial voltage decays with time constant RC. If the capacitor already starts in thermal equilibrium, its initial variance supplies the missing exponentially decaying term and the total variance stays constant.

Gain drift, interference and insufficient observation time also limit the inference. Linear filter

Words: 2k Articles: 16
Signal processing OurBigBook.com
A linear filter obeys the superposition principle: filtering αx+βz gives αT[x]+βT[z]. Many familiar examples are also linear time-invariant systems, represented by an impulse response and convolution. Linearity alone does not imply time invariance: multiplying x[n] by the index n is linear but changes its behavior when the same input is shifted.
The moving average is a finite impulse response example implemented by arithmetic; a band-pass filter can instead be built from a series RLC circuit. Their frequency responses explain which oscillations pass through. Choosing a filter means choosing how much amplitude, timing and detail may change, not simply removing every visible fluctuation.

Linear filter OurBigBook.com
For a linear time-invariant system, a sinusoidal wanted signal at ωs​ and an unwanted sinusoidal component at ωn​ acquire their separate frequency response factors. The ratio of their output amplitudes, divided by their input amplitude ratio, is η=∣H(ωn​)∣/∣H(ωs​)∣. An amplitude attenuation factor of F=1/η corresponds to a factor F2 in squared-amplitude power ratios under a common impedance convention. The unwanted component's own absolute attenuation is ∣H(ωn​)∣, which need not equal its attenuation relative to the wanted signal.

Low-pass filter

Words: 1k Articles: 9
Linear filter OurBigBook.com
A low-pass filter preferentially transmits low frequencies and attenuates higher frequencies. It can smooth rapid noise in a slowly varying signal, but it also suppresses wanted variations outside the useful signal bandwidth. An RC low-pass filter gives a concrete continuous-time example; a moving average implements related smoothing on a discrete-time signal.
The useful question is how much change the measurement can tolerate. Preserving the low frequencies of a temperature record while reducing a fast unwanted oscillation can improve readability. Preserving the sharp onset of a pulse requires higher frequencies, so excessive smoothing changes its timing and shape. The RC low-pass frequency response and RC low-pass step response make this signal bandwidth versus settling time tradeoff quantitative.

Low-pass filter OurBigBook.com
An RC low-pass filter places a resistor R>0 between input and output, with a capacitor C>0 from output to their common return. The ideal model prescribes the input electric potential difference and leaves the output unloaded. It is a first-order low-pass filter with unit eventual gain.[ref]
For electrical resistance R and capacitance C, Ohm's law gives the electric current through the resistor as (vin​−vout​)/R. The capacitor relation gives Cdvout​/dt. Equating them by Kirchhoff's current law yields the ordinary differential equation
RCdtdvout​​+vout​=vin​,τ=RC.
(71)
The time constant τ has units of time. A rapid change in electric potential difference requires a large electric current into the capacitor; the finite electrical resistance limits that rate. A slowly maintained voltage instead lets the capacitor approach the input voltage. The same equation therefore predicts both smoothing of sustained oscillations and a rounded response to a sudden change.
For the original constructed example throughout this article, take
R=2.2kΩ,C=47nF,τ=103.4μs.
(72)
These stipulated ideal values specify an analytical model, rather than measurements of particular components.

The two-channel setup can also test the predicted phase difference directly: for positive frequency f, measure the output's time lag Δt between corresponding features of the two sinusoids. For this single-stage model the phase lies between −π/2 and 0, so choose the lag within a quarter cycle and calculate ϕ=−2πfΔt. At the cutoff frequency the predicted lag is one eighth of a cycle. This tests the timing part of the frequency response as well as the voltage ratio.

A causal filter uses only present and past input values to produce its current output. The trailing moving average is causal; a centered average that uses future samples is not. Future samples can be available when processing a finished recording, but they are unavailable to a live measurement at the current time.

y[n]=∑j=0M−1​h[j]x[n−j].

This is a finite discrete convolution. The coefficients h[j] specify the complete operation; they need not be positive or equal. Such a filter has a simple bounded-input estimate, ∣y[n]∣≤∥x∥∞​∑j​∣h[j]∣, so bounded inputs remain bounded. The moving average chooses h[j]=1/M.

x[n]=sin(2π(0.025)n)+0.45sin(2π(0.2)n),
(84)
defined at every integer index. The first component completes one cycle in forty samples and the second in five. Averaging five consecutive samples cancels the second component exactly. The first becomes
y[n]=Asin(2π(0.025)(n−2)),A=5sin(π(0.025))sin(5π(0.025))​≈0.975498.
(85)
The remaining component is slightly smaller and delayed by two samples; the filter does not recover the original component unchanged.
The example is in steady operation: its early output values use the specified negative-index samples. Starting a device at n=0 with an unknown past requires an initialization rule. Treating earlier samples as zero, shortening the initial window, and postponing output until a full window is available produce different initial values.
For zero-mean uncorrelated random variables ε[n] with common variance σ2, the averaged disturbance has
Var(M1​∑j=0M−1​ε[n−j])=Mσ2​.
(86)
The standard deviation decreases by M​, but successive filtered errors share samples and are generally correlated. This variance calculation also assumes the wanted component is not damaged by averaging. A rapidly changing feature can be suppressed along with the disturbance.
The frequency response explains the cancellation and limits of this method. A moving average preserves low frequencies comparatively well, yet its side lobes make it a poor substitute for a sharply selective frequency cutoff. Smith develops this time-domain versus frequency-domain distinction in The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing, chapter 15: moving-average filters.

Band-pass filter

Words: 42
Linear filter OurBigBook.com
A band-pass filter preferentially transmits signals within a range of frequencies and attenuates sufficiently lower and higher frequencies. Taking the output voltage across the resistor in a series RLC circuit gives one example: the resonant series RLC response selects a band around 1/LC​. [ref].

Cutoff frequency (fc​)

Words: 25
Linear filter OurBigBook.com
A chosen boundary in a frequency response, commonly where the voltage amplitude gain falls to 1/2​ of its pass-region value. The convention must specify the reference gain.

Linear time-invariant system

Words: 443 Articles: 2
Signal processing OurBigBook.com
A linear time-invariant system combines two properties. Linearity means that the output from a linear combination of inputs is the same linear combination of their outputs. Time invariance means that shifting an input by an integer delay shifts its output by exactly that delay. The operation has no preference for a particular time origin.
For discrete time, write the unit impulse as δ[n]=1 at n=0 and zero otherwise, a Kronecker delta. Its response h[n]=T[δ][n] is the impulse response. A finite input can be decomposed into shifted impulses, giving
x[n]=∑k​x[k]δ[n−k]⟹y[n]=∑k​x[k]h[n−k]=(x∗h)[n].
(87)
The superposition principle supplies the sum and time invariance supplies the shifted copies of h. Infinite sums need convergence assumptions; for a bounded input and an impulse response h with absolute summability, the discrete convolution converges absolutely. For a physical system with stored initial energy, this construction describes the response with zero initial state; a separate free response accounts for nonzero initial conditions.
The gain is reuse. Measure or calculate one impulse response, and the convolution predicts the response to every allowed signal without solving a new dynamical problem each time. Alternatively, the frequency response predicts how each oscillatory component changes. [ref].

Frequency response (H(ω)=∑j​h[j]e−iωj)

Words: 263 Articles: 1
Linear time-invariant system OurBigBook.com
The frequency response gives the change in complex amplitude of a sustained oscillation under a linear time-invariant system. If the impulse response is finite or has absolute summability, substituting x[n]=eiωn into its discrete convolution yields
y[n]=∑j​h[j]eiω(n−j)=H(ω)eiωn,H(ω)=∑j​h[j]e−iωj.
(88)
Thus ∣H(ω)∣ is the amplitude gain and its complex argument is the phase change. Real sinusoids follow by taking real or imaginary parts. Here ω is radians per sample; ω=2πf for f cycles per sample. A physical sampling rate converts that normalized frequency into cycles per second.
For a trailing moving average,
H(ω)=M1​∑j=0M−1​e−iωj=e−iω(M−1)/2Msin(ω/2)sin(Mω/2)​,
(89)
with removable singularities evaluated from the finite sum. In particular H(0)=1. For M=5 and ω=2π/5, the five roots of unity sum to zero, so the oscillation is canceled. At small positive frequencies in the first pass region, the real sine ratio is positive and the phase factor gives a delay of (M−1)/2 samples.
Increasing M moves the first zero to ω=2π/M, narrowing the main region of large gain. It does not create an ideal low-frequency cutoff: later side lobes transmit some higher-frequency components, and suppressing a component is only helpful when that component is unwanted. The frequency plot is the same operation as the delayed-sample average; the five-vector diagram explains one exact zero geometrically.
Antiresonance
Words: 46
Frequency response OurBigBook.com
An antiresonance is a suppression of a specified measured response through cancellation of contributions, often between normal modes. It does not generally mean that the entire system is motionless. In an ideal undamped two-oscillator system, the directly driven oscillator can have zero displacement while its partner still moves.

Slotted line

Words: 31
Electrical engineering OurBigBook.com
A slotted line samples an electromagnetic field along a guide with a movable probe introduced through a longitudinal slot. Positions of standing wave minima determine the guided wavelength; a detector response need not be a calibrated field amplitude.

Telecommunication

Words: 2k Articles: 12
Electrical engineering OurBigBook.com
Telecommunication conveys information between separated places by physical signals. Radio communication uses radio waves; telegraphy communicates discrete written symbols. The engineering problem includes choosing a source, a channel and a readable output, then distinguishing that output from noise.

Telegraphy

Words: 37
Telecommunication OurBigBook.com
Telegraphy represents written symbols by agreed sequences of distinguishable signals. In wireless telegraphy, a key can select short and long transmission intervals; a receiver must recover their timing, rather than reproduce every rapid electrical oscillation as a visible mark.

Radio communication

Words: 2k Articles: 10
Telecommunication OurBigBook.com
Radio communication conveys information using radio waves coupled into and out of space by antennas. Amplitude modulation and frequency modulation vary a carrier wave; wireless telegraphy can instead encode symbols in transmission intervals. The useful separation is between the rapid electrical oscillation and the slower message timing. A receiver needs both frequency selection and a way to turn its selected signal into a readable output.

Radio transmitter

Words: 9
Radio communication OurBigBook.com
A radio transmitter drives an antenna to emit controlled radio waves.

Radio receiver

Words: 16
Radio communication OurBigBook.com
A radio receiver selects and detects an incoming radio wave; its frequency selection affects which signals reach its output.

Wireless telegraphy

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Radio communication OurBigBook.com
Wireless telegraphy conveys discrete symbols without a connecting message wire. Here the mechanism is radio communication: keyed excitation produces radio waves, a receiving antenna drives a selective electrical circuit, and a detector produces a readable event. This makes a beautiful bridge between resonance and information: accumulating many appropriately timed small electrical disturbances can distinguish one transmission from another. Selectivity is finite, however; resonance alone cannot guarantee immunity to strong unwanted signals or noise.
The 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics recognized Guglielmo Marconi and Karl Ferdinand Braun for contributions to wireless telegraphy.[ref] Their apparatus should be understood as a developing collection of systems. An early coherer receiver, a later tuned receiver and a modern envelope detector are different instruments.
Coherer
Words: 64
Wireless telegraphy OurBigBook.com
A filings coherer changes from high to low electrical resistance following electrical excitation. A local battery supplies the readout electric current; a tap resets the detector. It records events rather than the incident radio wave waveform.
Marconi described nickel and silver filings between silver plugs, with a cell and sensitive telegraph relay controlling a tapper and recorder.[ref]
Telegraph relay
Words: 40
Wireless telegraphy OurBigBook.com
A telegraph relay uses a small control electric current to switch a separate local electrical circuit. The recording mechanism's energy can therefore come from its own battery, rather than from the weak received signal. A sensitive trigger and a powerful readout serve different functions.
Tuned spark wireless apparatus
Words: 269 Articles: 1
Wireless telegraphy OurBigBook.com
Guglielmo Marconi's 1909 lecture describes antennas with earth connections and separate coupled receiving circuits. His 1900 system coupled a closed capacitor–inductor–spark gap loop to a transmitting antenna. Coil spacing adjusted coupling; inductance and capacitance adjusted tuning. All four circuits were tuned together. By 1909 his company's stations mainly used magnetic receivers, rather than coherers.[ref]
Those are a participant's retrospective descriptions, not a complete account of priority. An earth connection is part of this antenna arrangement; it is not a universal requirement for radio communication. Nor does tuning an isolated LC circuit ensure that its frequency remains unchanged when strongly coupled to another circuit. The coupled resonant circuit model quantifies that distinction.
Braun's receiver coupling experiment
Words: 156
Tuned spark wireless apparatus OurBigBook.com
In his 1909 lecture, Karl Ferdinand Braun recalled two experimental stations on Strasbourg forts in summer 1902. Known capacitances and calculated inductances set the transmitter tuning; the receiver searched for its two coupled oscillations. Its receiving coil fed a second coil in a tuned indicator circuit. Separating these coils increased both the sharpness of resonance and excitation intensity, until further separation reduced the response. The varied coil spacing was the control; transmitter coupling need not be loose for this receiver effect. For intensity measurements, Braun described an air-thermometer readout in the related resonant measuring apparatus.[ref]
The comparison tests receiver coupling, not an unrestricted law that looser coupling always helps. The paragraph does not identify the particular indicator used in the coil-spacing test or give a response curve from which to reconstruct its optimum. The plotted curves below are an original linear model with stated losses, rather than invented historical measurements.
Spark-excited damped oscillation (q(t)=Ae−αtcos(ωd​t+ϕ))
Words: 214
Wireless telegraphy OurBigBook.com
A spark gap can rapidly discharge a charged capacitor through an inductor. After excitation, the stored energy runs down through Joule heating, radiation and other losses. A key held down can permit repeated discharges: each discharge starts a damped train of rapid oscillations. The spark repetition frequency, the electrical oscillation frequency within each train, and the rate of keyed symbols are different quantities. Repetition does not make each train a maintained sinusoid.
An original lumped model replaces the conducting spark gap and other losses by a constant total electrical resistance R>0 in an isolated series RLC circuit. For electric charge q on the capacitor, the Kirchhoff cycle law gives
Lq¨​+Rq˙​+Cq​=0,ω0​=LC​1​,α=2LR​,Q=Rω0​L​.
(90)
For Q>1/2, its characteristic roots are −α±iωd​, with ωd​=ω02​−α2​, proving the stated damped form. The electric current q˙​ has the same exponential decay scale. Its wave envelope falls by exp(−2πα/ωd​) per cycle; the energy envelope falls twice as fast in the exponent. A maintained sinusoid instead requires continuing input power balancing losses.
With L=5mH, C=2nF and R=100Ω, the model gives f0​=ω0​/(2π)=50.329kHz, Q factor Q=15.811, amplitude time constant 1/α=100μs, and damped frequency ωd​/(2π)=50.304kHz. These are chosen component values. A real spark gap switches nonlinearly, an antenna radiates, and coupling exchanges energy between circuits; one constant-R free decay does not model the complete transmitter. Rapid damping also broadens the frequency spectrum, which helps explain why short trains make sharp receiver selection difficult.
Coupled resonant circuit demonstration
Words: 733 Articles: 1
Wireless telegraphy OurBigBook.com
MIT's demonstration places two 120-turn coils face to face, each with a capacitor. A swept sinusoid drives one circuit; an oscilloscope observes the other circuit's capacitor electric potential difference. The sheet specifies L=5mH and C=3300 or 2500pF, giving nominal resonant frequencies near 39 and 45kHz. It presents a procedure, not a measured dataset.[ref]
A reproducible extension can test the same selection principle with the identical components of the coupled resonant circuit model. Prepare two separate series loops, measure their actual inductances, capacitances and coil electrical resistances, and include generator Thévenin resistance in the driven loop's total R1​. Choose added resistors to make R1​=R2​=100Ω if the measured losses permit it. Include a known Rs​=50Ω sense resistor within R2​. Drive the first loop with a small function generator sinusoid; read the second loop's electric current as ∣I2​∣=∣U∣/Rs​ using an oscilloscope across the sense resistor. Here U denotes the sense reading, distinct from the source electric potential difference V in the model.
Sweep 35–68kHz slowly enough for transients to settle; record source frequency, source amplitude at the circuit terminals, and sense amplitude. Repeat at fixed coil spacing after changing one capacitor, then at fixed components after changing spacing. Turn the drive off to establish the background; rotate the receiving coil toward a right angle to test inductive coupling; restore its orientation and repeat to check drift. These are proposed controls, not observations reported by MIT. Keep probe loading small and account for it if not negligible. A grounded oscilloscope can electrically join the loops if attached to both: use an appropriately isolated differential input for any simultaneous primary measurement, or measure the primary separately.
Recovering deliberately chosen long and short generator bursts on the receiver trace demonstrates symbol timing. The essential inference is narrower than a long-distance radio test: nearby coils primarily exchange energy through mutual inductance in the near and far field regime dominated by the near field. Coil spacing, detuning and background controls distinguish this coupling from a direct wire connection or incidental pickup. They do not by themselves demonstrate reception of propagating radio waves in the radiation zone.
Coupled resonant circuit model (M=kL1​L2​​)
Words: 399
Coupled resonant circuit demonstration OurBigBook.com
Let two series loops have inductances L1​,L2​>0, capacitances C1​,C2​>0, total electrical resistances R1​,R2​>0, and reciprocal mutual inductance M=kL1​L2​​ with 0≤k<1. For a steady sinusoid of angular frequency ω>0, choose complex peak amplitudes with time convention eiωt. An ideal source of peak electric potential difference V drives loop 1; loop 2 has no independent source. Then
Zj​=Rj​+i(ωLj​−ωCj​1​),(Z1​iωM​iωMZ2​​)(I1​I2​​)=(V0​),VI2​​=Z1​Z2​+ω2M2−iωM​.
(91)
Eliminating I1​ proves the response formula. Reversing one coil changes the sign of M and the relative wave phase, but leaves this amplitude response unchanged. The measured sense ratio is ∣Rs​I2​/V∣, with Rs​ included in R2​, not added a second time.
For identical loops at their uncoupled resonant frequency ω0​=1/LC​,
​VI2​​​ω0​​=R2+ω02​M2ω0​M​.
(92)
Writing x=ω0​M/R makes this x/[R(1+x2)]. Its derivative has the sign of 1−x2, so response at this fixed frequency is largest when x=1, equivalently k=1/Q. Too little coupling transfers little excitation; excessive coupling reduces the response at the original centre frequency. This is a fixed-frequency optimum, not a universal optimum over every possible receiver and drive frequency.
For the chosen values, k=1/Q=0.063246 gives M=0.31623mH. At source peak V=0.100V, the secondary peak electric current is 0.500mA and the sense peak electric potential difference is 25.0mV. The primary peak electric current is also 0.500mA, so source mean power is 25.0μW: each loop dissipates 12.5μW, checking conservation of energy. Here V is the equivalent ideal source behind R1​; a generator's terminal reading must be converted using its measured Thévenin resistance.
In the lossless identical-loop limit, the normal modes have equal or opposite electric currents, making their effective inductances L+M or L−M. Thus
flow​=1+k​f0​​,fhigh​=1−k​f0​​.
(93)
At k=0.20 these are 45.944 and 56.270kHz. Finite electrical resistance broadens and shifts the driven peaks, so the exact response formula, rather than these lossless values, generates the plot. Changing a capacitor moves the uncoupled tuning through f0​∝C−1/2: increasing it by 21% lowers f0​ by the factor 1/1.1. The model explains why tuning and coupling must be adjusted together; it supplies no transatlantic propagation or detector-threshold prediction.
